about.title: Lodi Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Lodi's mix of downtown storefronts, shopping centers along Kettleman Lane, and residential complexes near Cherokee Lane and Lower Sacramento Road means plenty of foot traffic across privately owned and managed spaces. When a wet floor, broken stair, uneven walkway, or poorly lit parking area causes a fall, the property owner's responsibility often comes down to whether they knew—or reasonably should have known—about the hazard and failed to address it. That's a fact-specific question, and it depends heavily on what evidence exists: photos of the condition, surveillance footage, incident reports, and witness accounts. LawProactive doesn't practice law or represent you directly. We simply connect you with an independent, California-licensed attorney in our network who can review what happened and explain your options. There's no cost to get connected, and if the attorney takes your case, they generally work on contingency, meaning no fee unless you recover something.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Lodi Premises Case

items.title: Proving Notice
items.desc: California law generally requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and didn't fix or warn about it. An attorney can help identify what evidence supports that timeline.

items.title: Video Doesn't Wait
items.desc: Many Lodi retailers and apartment complexes overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can matter.

items.title: Comparative Fault Considerations
items.desc: California applies pure comparative fault, meaning your recovery can be reduced by your share of responsibility but isn't automatically barred. An attorney can help address how a property owner might argue you contributed to the fall.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip-and-fall claim in Lodi?
items.answer: Generally, California allows two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit for a private property claim. If the fall happened on public property, such as a city sidewalk near downtown Lodi, the deadline is much shorter and involves a separate claims process. Speaking with an independent attorney early helps make sure you don't miss a critical window.

items.question: What if I fell in a Lodi store and there's no incident report?
items.answer: An incident report isn't required for a claim to move forward, though it can help. What matters more is documenting the scene yourself if possible—photos of the hazard, your shoes, and the surrounding area—and identifying any witnesses. An attorney can also request the store's internal records and surveillance footage.

items.question: Do I need to prove the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, in most cases California law requires showing the owner had actual or constructive notice of the dangerous condition and a reasonable opportunity to fix or warn about it. This is often the most contested part of a premises case. An independent attorney can help evaluate what evidence exists to support that notice.
